h: Not just votes, two thousand crore left people’s pockets
dek: The bill for 13 crore names cut is not only about democracy. It is about the treasury too. The writer says the Election Commission does not disclose its spending, and ordinary people are paying the bill.
body: The moment SIR is mentioned, the debate stops at politics. Nobody remembers the money. The writer's question is direct: what does this exercise cost, and whose pocket is it coming out of? Thirteen crore names have been cut, twelve lakh government employees are knocking on doors, and workers are going back to their own states after losing a full month's wages.

The Commission's own budget is small. It was Rs 304.98 crore last year, and has gone up 25.33 per cent this time. But one SIR cycle burns thousands of crore, and that money comes through the Ministry of Law. The bigger share of the burden sits on the states. Telangana estimated 200 crore, of which 85 crore was for BLOs and officers alone. Bengal's budget was 450 crore, and it crossed 500 crore, and many BLOs got 5,000 instead of the promised 12,000.

The result shows in the rolls. In Delhi's 31 August draft list, out of 1.45 crore voters only 97.53 lakh remained, which means 32.78 per cent of names were cut. A process meant to take two or three months ran for eleven months. In Bengal, 27 lakh people could not vote. The writer reminds us that money was first spent on cutting names, then the same money on adding them back, and neither account is recorded anywhere.

By the Sabar Institute's estimate, about 1,983 crore rupees went out of people's pockets. One and a half crore voters were called to hearings after tribunal notices; the fare, the food and the lost wages were all their own. One elderly man had to spend at least 250 rupees a day to prove he was alive.

The Commission now says that in the remaining 17 states it will hold a normal summary revision instead of SIR. At the end the writer asks whether this amounts to admitting a mistake, and whether the young people who demanded a resignation were right.
nazar: The SIR bill arrives in two places: on the Constitution, and on the ration plate. When a name is cut, it is not only the vote that goes. A scheme, a bank account and school attendance are also at stake.
In our view, election reform should begin with one simple thing: every state's SIR spending must be made public, so that it becomes clear who is finally paying the bill for cleaning up democracy.
sawal: If the poor pay the bill for the clean-up, who is the clean-up for?
ref: Sabar Institute
A small research institute in Kolkata that gathers voter-list data and works out the count of names removed.
BLO
Booth Level Officer, usually a schoolteacher, given the duty of going door to door to hand out forms.
ank: Names removed from the voter list
Money that went out of people's pockets

h: The rally was big, the threat is not: why is Modi in such a hurry?
dek: The writer says the opposition has no evidence yet that it can turn this issue into votes. So why is the Prime Minister talking about a foreign hand and anarchy?
body: Sunday's rally was big. The mood was hot and the speeches were loud. The writer believes this left Home Minister Amit Shah unmoved. Electoral wisdom says that bringing a few lakh workers to Delhi can be a show of strength, but it is not a measure of electoral strength.

The writer offers his own examples. A year before the Bengal election the Left parties held a huge rally at Brigade Parade Ground in Kolkata, with lakhs of people. The result was one seat in a 294-member assembly. In Bihar, Rahul Gandhi's vote theft campaign did not take off. In Karnataka, in the two seats where Rahul showed proof of names being cut, the Congress drew a blank in four Legislative Council seats, and lost the Bengaluru teachers' seat as well.

So why did the Prime Minister come out with such a big answer? On Saturday, without naming anyone, Modi asked who was meeting whom secretly abroad, and which anti-India forces were with them. The writer says this is the language of panic. The man who was mocked as Pappu until yesterday is now said to be spreading anarchy. Indira Gandhi chose exactly this language for Jayaprakash Narayan.

The real worry is Gen Z. In Sri Lanka, Bangladesh and Nepal a new generation has pulled governments down. In Serbia the students' Student List won an election, and its parliament was called the most educated parliament in the world, even though the movement had no face. In India the Cockroach Janta Party set the mood, but students came out on their own in Mumbai and Patna.

This is where the writer's warning lies. Parties stepping into this mood is a risk for the opposition too, because it takes away the movement's innocence and the movement can dissolve into old party politics. The next Lok Sabha election is two and a half years away, and the opposition's priorities do not take long to change.
nazar: A crowd and a vote count are two different things, and that is true. But it is also true that the people whose names were cut were forced to carry their complaint to the street before they could reach the court's door.
The panic in power should not be taken lightly. When a government starts calling peaceful dissent a foreign conspiracy, the issue stops being only about seats. It becomes about the right to speak.
sawal: If vote theft does not turn into votes, what is the government afraid of?
ref: Brigade Parade Ground
A large ground in Kolkata, where the Left Front held a huge rally in 2025 and then won a single seat.
Legislative Council election
Elections held through graduates' and teachers' constituencies, seen as a measure of a party's urban and educated base.

h: For those who warned in 2019, the stage is empty
dek: The writer asks that if the movement is against names being cut, why is there silence about the law that set this machine running.
body: Nearly thirteen crore names have been cut from the voter list. Opposition parties, students and farmers are on the street, demanding the election commissioner's resignation. The writer does not oppose this, but her eye is on the old warning that Muslims gave six years ago: if you tie citizenship to papers, they will be the first to be pushed out. Now the danger has reached everyone, so the streets are full.

In December 2019 came the citizenship amendment law, which gives a fast track to citizenship for people of six religions and leaves Islam out. Amit Shah had said in Kolkata that the sequence should be understood: first the citizenship law, then the National Register of Citizens. That same winter, women sat down in Shaheen Bagh.

Now the same paper is being asked for at another office. In Bihar, the SIR order came on 24 June 2025, and it also spoke of adding the names of infiltrators to the list. Two birth dates, 1 July 1987 and 2 December 2004, became the test, and in the Supreme Court the Commission's lawyer said this was a citizenship check under the 2003 amendment. In other words, the voter list itself is becoming the citizenship register.

In Bengal, 91 lakh names were cut before the vote, 12 per cent. In the second round, 60 lakh people were sent to judicial officers, where the decision rested on the officer's discretion. 27 lakh names were removed, and about 70 per cent of them were identified as Muslim from their surnames, though Muslims are about a quarter of the state's population. According to the Sabar Institute, Muslims had been more successful in adding their families to the old list.

In Delhi, the 31 August draft list cut 47.5 lakh names out of 1.45 crore, 45 per cent in Okhla and 42 per cent in Patel Nagar. The opposition's demands speak of saving genuine voters from technical errors. The writer asks: what about that voter whom the state itself has refused to accept as genuine?
nazar: This piece is a criticism of its own side, and that is why it matters. A movement that is angry only about its own cut names, and does not remember those whose names were cut earlier, travels only half the way.

In our view, the most dangerous part of SIR is its back door, which leads from the voter list to a citizenship check. The demand to shut that door should be part of the movement, or the same machine will return next time under a new name.
sawal: Whose patent is on the machine that cut the names?
ref: Shaheen Bagh
A women's sit-in in Delhi in December 2019 against the citizenship law, which ran all winter.
Infiltrator
In politics this word has usually been used for Bangladeshi Muslims.

h: Two days, one point: vote theft is now everybody's issue
dek: The paper's view: Saturday's impeachment and Sunday's rally kept the whole country's debate on a single agenda for two days.
body: The rally of about two dozen parties led by the Congress at Ramlila Maidan on Sunday was splendid and full of life in itself, there is no doubt. The paper writes that even those who will not accept it accept it inside; they may not admit it with their tongue, but their heart must testify that the ground was full.

But the paper does not look at it alone. It is linked to the meeting held a day earlier at Kharge's residence, which can be called a maha ajlas. There, MPs of all opposition parties gathered over the impeachment of the election commissioner, and in an effective move the first day's session was stretched into the second day. On the first day, MPs, civil society people and those citizens whose names had been cut from the vote took part.

The second day had a gathering of party workers and ordinary people who see vote theft as an attack on the Constitution. According to the paper, Saturday's people's impeachment created the mood for Sunday's rally, and it cannot be denied that the first day added to the second day's energy.

In this way the country saw that the opposition is united, and so are the people. An understanding is forming that vote theft is not a matter of one seat, one community or one party, and those not cut today can be cut tomorrow. The paper's charge is clear: the aim is to build a one-party system and make elections meaningless.

The paper congratulates the opposition, civil society, student organisations, lawyers and content creators for taking this message to people in a way that even supporters of the ruling party looked uneasy. Rahul Gandhi said this was everybody's march and everybody's rally. The paper's conclusion: keeping the issue in discussion for two days is enough to show that it will have an effect on the opposition's election campaign.
nazar: The editorial is right that holding one issue for two days is a political victory in itself. But unity on the stage and unity at the booth are two different things.
The real test will come when the fight is to add names back, with forms, dates and rounds of offices. There it is organisation that counts, not speeches.
sawal: Two dozen parties on the stage, but who will do the counting at the booth?
ref: Maha ajlas
A large gathering in Urdu. Inquilab gave this name to the opposition session at Kharge's residence.
Impeachment
Here it means the constitutional process for removing the election commissioner, which the opposition repeated in symbolic form.

h: The same ground, the map turned around: 2014 was built from here
dek: Column: from the Ramlila Maidan that gave the BJP political support twelve years ago, the opposition showed its strength against it on Sunday.
body: The writer says time has completed a circle. The players have changed, the ground is the same. Delhi's Ramlila Maidan, which became the centre of the 2011 anti-corruption movement, on Sunday witnessed a completely different scene.

From that same ground the BJP took political advantage by standing behind Anna Hazare's movement. Now, at the same place, opposition parties led by the Congress came out united against the BJP government. At the INDIA bloc rally, 21 parties were on the stage, along with civil society representatives, several of whom had been at the front of the anti-corruption movement after 2010.

According to the writer, the presence of CPI(M) and CPI(ML) workers was notable, because both parties had supported the Anna movement. This time general secretary M.A. Baby and Dipankar Bhattacharya spoke from the stage. Baby said Modi is an emperor of lies, and that everyone would have to fight a united battle to end vote theft and save democracy and the Constitution.

Between 2014 and 2026 politics turned almost 180 degrees. Communal politics became normal, the relatively free media knelt before power, and a capitalism tied to big businessmen became the identity of the economy. The Congress changed too: the party that was under pressure from the anti-corruption movement yesterday is today the biggest force in the opposition fight against the BJP.

Rahul Gandhi understands this change best, perhaps because he has lived through it. In twelve years he was attacked continuously and mocked on social media. When he stood up to speak on the stage, the whole ground echoed with slogans and clapping, and he called the rally Shiva's wedding procession. Farmers from Haryana told the writer that they had been warning for years but people did not listen. Adivasi women from Chhattisgarh said Rahul takes everyone along, while the BJP has divided people.
nazar: This comparison is not only a fondness for old memories. It is a question too: if the anger on the street could change power in 2011, why can the anger of 2026 not change it? The difference is that then the opposition and a large part of the media were on the same side.
The real legacy of Ramlila Maidan is that a crowd does not wait. Those who repeat old speeches can stand there, but only those who fight the daily battle of getting names added will last.
sawal: Power changed in 2011, so why not in 2026?
ref: Anna movement
The movement against corruption that ran from Delhi in 2011-12, with Ramlila Maidan as its centre.
Shiva's wedding procession
The name Rahul Gandhi gave the rally; in the old story, gods, ghosts and gandharvas all walk together in Shiva's wedding procession.

h: After the rally, what does the Congress have left, a crowd or only a crowd
dek: The ground was full and the crowd reached Minto Road. But two senior journalists see it differently: one reads a message, the other sees the real test still ahead.
body: At ten in the morning the traffic near Minto Bridge was normal. Workers of the Congress, the Samajwadi Party and other opposition parties had begun to gather, and at that point it was hard to guess how big the crowd would grow by afternoon. The BBC team recorded that this time Samajwadi Party workers were more visible than at earlier protests, and they had come not only from western Uttar Pradesh but from distant districts of eastern UP as well.

Around half past one in the afternoon Rahul Gandhi passed under Minto Bridge in an open bus, with Akhilesh Yadav beside him in the same bus. The crowd was so large that getting inside the ground took real effort. Hands held posters with Gyanesh Kumar's face, and the slogans attacked him and the Prime Minister directly.

The crowd was not only of parties, and that was the most interesting thing about this rally. A Congress worker who came from Gujarat said that now it is not only workers, ordinary people are coming in large numbers too. A software engineer said she is not with any party, but the issue is so serious that she had to come.

Senior journalist Sharad Gupta's assessment is that the roads and the ground looked full, and the opposition succeeded in sending a message against the government. He says the opposition, which was not able to push its demand inside the House, placed that demand before the people through this event.

Senior journalist Ramkripal Singh has a different question. He says crowds have come to opposition rallies before too, so the real test is how the parties' coordination moves forward after that crowd, and how far the Congress can strengthen its own position. Being angry with the government and accepting another party as an alternative are different things. In his view the anger will count only when people see the Congress as the alternative, and for that the organisation will have to be strengthened.
nazar: This report does not decide on its own, and that is its strength. The most honest question in crowd politics is always this: will the people in the ground today be standing at the booth in the next election or not.
In our view the rally's solid work was that it took the issue out of TV debates and carried it to the lanes and neighbourhoods. The rest is the organisation's job, and that is not built by speeches.
sawal: What will the crowd's energy turn into by the next election?
ref: Minto Bridge
A bridge over the railway line in the middle of Delhi, from where the road to Ramlila Maidan goes.
Ramkripal Singh
A senior journalist who has written on party organisation and election strategy.

h: A rally does not produce a resignation: the three tests of court, Parliament and street
dek: The writer explains how steep the road to removing the chief election commissioner is, and how far the case in the Supreme Court can go.
body: Sunday's rally has brought the SIR question and Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar back into the headlines. But the writer says the rally is not the whole fight, only one part of it. Three paths lie ahead and each has its limits: a challenge in the Supreme Court to the way the Commission took its decisions, the removal process in Parliament, and keeping the movement alive after the rally.

In court the Commission has filed a 248-page counter affidavit. It says all three orders linked to SIR were taken with the consent of all three commissioners, and the charge of deciding alone is wrong. The Commission has also denied that it changed Form 6. It says the additional declaration asked for along with the form is a separate document.

The petitioners' question is about process, that is, that the record of how the decisions were taken should come out. The court has not yet ruled on the charges, nor has it heard the wider question of SIR's validity. So the next round is about examining the arguments of both sides, not a final verdict.

The parliamentary path is steeper still. Under Article 324(5), the chief election commissioner can be removed the same way as a Supreme Court judge. Article 124(4) says there must be proved misbehaviour or incapacity, and both Houses must pass an address in the same session. The motion needs a majority of the total membership of each House and a two-thirds majority of those present and voting.

A notice needs the support of at least 100 members in the Lok Sabha or at least 50 in the Rajya Sabha. The Speaker or the Chairman can accept or reject it. If it is accepted, a three-member committee holds an inquiry. The opposition's earlier notices were rejected on 6 April. The writer's conclusion is clear: a political demand and a constitutional process are not the same thing, and a rally or a symbolic motion cannot remove the commissioner from office.
nazar: This piece takes away hope, but it is necessary. The pressure of a movement works only when there is paper behind it: a record of every name cut, the date of every hearing and the result of every appeal.

In our view, arguing only about process in the Supreme Court is not enough. The court will also have to decide whether turning the voter list into a tool for citizenship checks sits inside the Constitution or not.
sawal: The court will look at process. Who will stop the citizenship check?
ref: Article 324(5)
A provision of the Constitution that makes removing the chief election commissioner as hard as removing a Supreme Court judge.
Judges (Inquiry) Act, 1968
The law that sets out how notices against judges, the inquiry committee and the process work; the same route applies here.

h: A census of idlis and chairs, not of voters
dek: Drones, AI and even leftover idlis were counted to measure the rally crowd, but nobody asked for a count of the voters cut from the rolls.
body: As the Ramlila Maidan rally broke up on 1 November, a second rally began. This time some people walked into the ground with cameras and started counting the empty chairs. Some sat on the chairs and had their pictures taken, some counted them. In TV studios every empty patch of the ground became a big discovery.

The argument was only about numbers. The organisers claimed lakhs of people, while the other side struggled to bring it down to thousands. Someone claimed seven lakh idlis were ordered, two idlis and a chutney packet each, and because the crowd did not come, lakhs of packets were left over. The writer asks who kept the account of this idli stock, and when the leftover chutney will get its own inquiry.

Then a supporter had ChatGPT count the people after watching a 75-second drone video. The answer came back: 30,000 to 35,000 people inside the ground. The same answer also added the police estimate of 60,000 to 70,000, including those standing outside. In other words, a short drone video was treated as a census.

The writer also accepts that the claim of ten lakh is worth checking; leaders always inflate crowd figures. The question is why so much effort went into proving only that nobody came. He says this is the unease of the counters themselves, who stayed stuck in the rally even after it was over.

At the end the writer suggests that the calculators count something else now: how many more votes were polled in past elections, how many voters' names were removed from the rolls on purpose, how much the price of pulses and vegetables rose, how many corruption cases surfaced. These numbers are tied to people's lives, not to empty chairs and leftover idlis. The question is whether counting is fun only when the numbers belong to the opposition.
nazar: Our politics and our TV are both stuck on counting crowds. Whether a rally's number is inflated or cut down becomes a subject of debate, but when the account of names cut from the voter list is demanded, silence falls.
Government or opposition, both should publish their own numbers, so that the job of counting is not left to drones and ChatGPT.
sawal: Those counting chairs, when will you count the list of cut voters?
ref: Counting crowds by drone
The practice of estimating numbers from aerial video after a rally, which is now also done with AI.
Seven lakh idlis
The claimed number of food packets ordered for the rally, which was presented as proof of a small crowd.

h: Ladakh: a promise of the Sixth Schedule, now a draft under Article 240
dek: The draft Delhi has sent will give Ladakh an elected body, but the power to run it will stay in Delhi's hands.
body: In August 2019 Article 370 was removed from Jammu and Kashmir, and the state was split into two union territories. Ladakh's people were then assured that it would be brought under the Sixth Schedule, like some tribal areas of the Northeast. The Sixth Schedule creates autonomous district councils, which can make their own laws on matters such as land and forests.

In February 2026 the government stepped back from that promise. A long movement followed, in which four protesters were killed in police firing in September 2025. In May 2026 an agreement was reached between the home ministry, the Ladakh Apex Body and the Kargil Democratic Alliance. It was settled that statehood would remain a long-term demand, but in the first step an elected body would be formed at the Ladakh level, with executive, financial and legislative powers. Article 371 was also to be considered.

On 15 October the home ministry sent a draft of the new legal status, which is much weaker than the May agreement. In it the elected body is created under Article 240, which is meant for union territories. The central government can change or remove Article 240 provisions on its own, with no need for a constitutional amendment.

There are other gaps. Rights over natural resources have been left out of the list, the budget will have to be made within its own allocation and sent to the Centre, central laws will continue to apply, and the lieutenant governor can dissolve the body at any time. The Ladakh Apex Body and the Kargil Democratic Alliance sent their reply on 19 October and recorded exactly these objections.

The writer also notes that the Centre has issued the Ladakh Autonomous Hill Development Councils (Amendment) Rules 2026 without talking to Ladakhi organisations, though the agreement had said no major step would be taken until the new status came into force. He says large projects are raising the risk of land being taken over.
nazar: Ladakh's fight is not only Ladakh's. When Delhi replaces its own promise with a flexible route like Article 240, it hits the trust of every region that was given a place in the Constitution through special status.

The real guarantee for a weak region is not a seal on a file. It is a right written in the Constitution. The more easily that can be changed, the weaker the trust between the country's different identities will be.
sawal: A body the lieutenant governor can dissolve is elected by whom?
ref: Article 240
The article of the Constitution that allows rules to be made for union territories; the central government can change these rules on its own.
Sixth Schedule
The arrangement that gives autonomous district councils to tribal areas of the Northeast, where the council holds rights over land and custom.

h: Bangladesh: not 12,500, the demand is 30,000 taka
dek: Garment workers are on the street, and the question is why the government waited until a December deadline to form the wage board.
body: Workers in Bangladesh's readymade garment industry are on the street in Dhaka and in factory areas outside it. Their demand is that the minimum monthly wage be raised from 12,500 taka to 30,000 taka. Days of protests have stopped production, damaged public and private property, and caused serious trouble for ordinary people.

The demand is not unreasonable. Inflation, rent, transport and everyday costs kept rising, while wages stayed where they were. According to the paper's reporting, there are also complaints of arbitrary dismissals and of workers being put on blacklists. The workers are asking not only for a fair wage but for decent conditions of work.

The question is why they had to come to the street. The government announced a new wage board on 15 October, but the process was not complete until Sunday, and by then the protest had already flared. The three-year review deadline runs out in December, so why the delay? The paper writes that if the board had been formed in time, matters would not have gone this far.

On Sunday protesters kept the Dhaka-Tangail highway closed for nearly six hours, and on Monday there was a long traffic jam again. Angered by a rumour that someone had been taken into custody, a crowd set fire to police vehicles and boxes, and police fired tear gas and water cannon. At least 529 factories in Mirpur, Savar, Ashulia, Gazipur and Mymensingh announced a holiday, and 25 people were injured in the violence in Gazipur.

The paper suggests that the government make the labour minister a permanent and accessible link between workers and owners, with both the power and the will to bring owners to the negotiating table. Such an arrangement should not take away the right to peaceful protest, but should reduce the need for it. At the same time, workers too should not make violence their everyday way of speaking.
nazar: The strongest part of Bangladesh's economy runs on the very hands whose wages have not risen in three years. When export figures are praised, it has to be decided who will get a share of the labour.
The condition of factory and contract workers here is no different. The lesson is that a negotiating table costs less than a street, but the table has to be set up in time.
sawal: Who keeps shutting the path that would raise wages without a march to the street?
ref: Wage board
The government body in Bangladesh that fixes the minimum wage, and has to review it every three years.
RMG
Readymade garments, meaning finished clothing; the industry brings in the largest share of Bangladesh's exports.

h: South Asia: trade with Brazil costs more than trade with a neighbour
dek: For an Indian company, doing business with Brazil is about 20 per cent cheaper than with a neighbouring country.
body: South Asia has a strange contradiction. It is among the most densely populated regions in the world, its markets are large, the average age is 27.8 years and its economies are growing fast. Yet the countries behave economically as if a sea lay between them.

Intra-regional trade is only 5 per cent of South Asia's total trade, while in ASEAN it is about 25 per cent and in Africa 16 per cent. The World Bank estimates this trade at about 23 billion dollars, when the potential is at least 67 billion dollars. Every year about 44 billion dollars turns into factories and jobs that were never built.

SAARC was created in Dhaka in 1985. In four decades it has produced declarations, committees and a free trade agreement like SAFTA, and the development fund set up in 2010 has approved more than 90 projects. But the effect on intra-regional trade has been very small. In 2003 a senior SAARC official himself called the organisation moribund.

The writer holds that the blame is not only India and Pakistan quarrelling. Pakistan has kept blocking integration in which India's dominance is accepted, and India has kept avoiding demands that would give smaller countries equal status. A former foreign secretary himself said that India had been stingy in investing in the regional framework and in opening its market.

According to the writer, the largest economy has to bear more of the cost at the start. India gains from reaching the Northeast through Bangladesh and from trade in energy. On the other side, Bangladesh, Nepal, Bhutan, Sri Lanka and the Maldives want the Indian market, but they also fear that dependence will shrink their freedom.
nazar: For India this question is the biggest, because the most is expected of the big neighbour. If India opens its market and its road and rail routes to smaller neighbours, its Northeast and border areas will gain first.
This path can work even without Pakistan. A start can be made with the countries already in talks, but the intent must be visible, or every neighbour will keep seeing Delhi as a bully.
sawal: If trade with a neighbour costs more, what is a neighbour for?
ref: SAFTA
The South Asian Free Trade Area agreement, in force since 2006, which aims to cut tariffs between member countries.
RCSS
The Regional Centre for Strategic Studies in Colombo, where this lecture was delivered on 26 October 2026.

h: Venezuela: the oil is its own, the vault belongs to America
dek: Even after Maduro is gone, oil earnings do not reach Venezuela's treasury. They are deposited in accounts watched by the United States.
body: A little after two in the morning on 3 January 2026, about 150 American aircraft struck Caracas. Air defences, communication antennas and military sites were the targets. During the same operation, commandos of the US Delta Force picked up President Nicolas Maduro and his wife Cilia Flores. Congress was not told in advance.

According to Venezuela's defence minister, 47 soldiers were killed, and Cuba reported the deaths of 32 of its people. Two civilians were also killed, including a Colombian street vendor, taking the total to about 80. Two days later Maduro was in a New York court, facing charges of narco-terrorism and a conspiracy to smuggle cocaine, and he pleaded not guilty.

He is now in a Brooklyn jail, and the trial will begin in June 2027. That means that for a year and a half a sovereign country's president will be held in an American jail without a trial. Trump said that same day that the United States would 'run' Venezuela until power is transferred, and called it his 'Monroe Doctrine'.

Power did not go to the opposition. Vice President Delcy Rodríguez became acting president on 5 January, and on 30 March the American embassy in Caracas reopened. Opposition leader María Corina Machado, who won the Nobel Peace Prize, had gifted her medal to Trump, and still did not get power. She returned on 25 October but was kept out of the talks.

On the oil front, a 9 January executive order sent the earnings into accounts under American watch and voided creditors' claims. More than 13 billion dollars has been deposited since January. In August a 25-year agreement was signed: 17 oil fields in a 65 billion barrel reserve, and 19 dollars to Venezuela for every barrel sold to the United States. On paper the oil is hers, but America gives the permission to spend it.
nazar: This story is not only Venezuela's. If the money of the country with the world's largest oil reserve can carry someone else's seal, then what the sovereignty of small countries is worth is still to be settled.
There is a lesson for India too. Our companies are buying oil there, but the deal is running on Washington's terms. Energy security holds only when no single country controls the source.
sawal: The oil is its own, so who fixed 19 dollars on every barrel?
ref: Monroe Doctrine
The 1823 American declaration that asked Europe to stay away from the western hemisphere; later the United States drew a right of intervention from it.
PDVSA
Venezuela's state oil company, through which the country's oil earnings used to be accounted for.

h: Europe's unease: China keeps its capitalists on a leash
dek: Macron called the October trade deal a victory, but the writer says Europe's real trouble comes from the structure of China's economy.
body: In October the European Union and China reached a deal aimed at reducing the 360 billion euro trade deficit with China. Macron called it a victory against 'unfair competition'. The deal speaks of cutting imports of Chinese hybrid cars.

The writer accepts that the Chinese challenge is real, but Europe's companies are not blameless either. Volkswagen handed shareholders 20 billion euros in three years and put no money into research on cheap electric cars. In the second quarter of 2026 profit fell 9.5 per cent to 3.5 billion euros. Four plants in Germany are now closing and a lakh jobs are being cut worldwide.

According to the writer, the real difficulty comes from China's political economy. Chinese state companies are 62 per cent of the total assets of state companies worldwide, while Europe's share is only 14 per cent. These companies do not run only for profit, so they can make expensive, long-term investments in power and rail.

The result shows in the figures. Industrial electricity in Europe costs twice what it does in America and 50 per cent more than in China. In 2023 China's public sector held 3.5 trillion dollars in listed equity, while Europe held 1.3 trillion dollars. In China, companies in which the state holds more than a quarter share own nearly half the market; in OECD countries that figure is 2 per cent.

The writer does not say Europe should copy China, because the burden of that race would fall on workers and on the planet. She says Europe should build its industries through public investment and turn big capital towards productive work. In the 2028 to 34 budget several countries want a 10 per cent real cut, while money is moving towards military spending.
nazar: This debate matters to us, because India too talks of building its industry with cheap electricity and public investment. The lesson is that tariffs and subsidies alone do not win a contest if public companies lack the nerve for long investments.

Second, like Europe we too will have to decide that spending on research and power matters more than handing out profit. Otherwise, after losing in foreign markets, the same story will repeat at home.
sawal: Why does Europe keep electricity expensive for its own industries?
ref: Trade deficit
When a country or bloc buys more goods from another than it sells, the gap is called a trade deficit; here it is 360 billion euros.
State enterprise
Companies owned by the government, which are the backbone of key sectors such as power, rail and finance in China.

h: Murasu heads for the Andhra coast, winds up to 120 kmph
dek: The weather office says the storm will make landfall between Nellore and Narsapur, with heavy rain alerts in four states.
body: According to the India Meteorological Department, the severe cyclonic storm Murasu, formed in the west-central Bay of Bengal, will make landfall on the Andhra Pradesh coast between midnight on 2 November and the morning of 3 November. The landfall is expected between Nellore and Narsapur, south of Ongole. Winds will blow at 100 to 110 kmph and gusts can reach 120 kmph.

The Doppler radars at Chennai, Machilipatnam and Visakhapatnam are tracking it continuously. Coastal Andhra Pradesh and Rayalaseema are expected to get heavy to very heavy rain on 2 and 3 November, and some places may get extremely heavy rain. Warnings have also been issued for Telangana, Tamil Nadu, Odisha and Kerala, and several states from Karnataka to Bihar may get rain.

In coastal Andhra and Yanam winds may blow at 80 to 90 kmph, with gusts up to 110. In the 24 hours to half past eight on the morning of 2 November, Tamil Nadu and central Maharashtra recorded 12 to 21 centimetres of rain, and Assam, Odisha and Kerala 7 to 11 centimetres. Murasu is a Tamil word for a large drum, long used for war, for festivals and to warn of danger.

The storm is arriving at a time when coastal areas have already been damaged by Arnab. Andhra Pradesh Chief Minister Chandrababu Naidu has cancelled his Monday trip to Delhi. Several flights are reported cancelled at Chennai airport.
nazar: After Arnab the roofs in coastal villages have still not been rebuilt, and Murasu is at the door. Announcing wind speeds is one thing. Calling fishermen back to harbour, emptying schools in advance and getting water and power to relief camps is another. Last week's damage shows there is still a big gap between warning and preparation.
sawal: Who repaired the roofs flattened by Arnab before Murasu came?
ref: Rayalaseema
The dry southern region of Andhra Pradesh, which gets little rain and is hit by drought again and again.
Doppler radar
A weather department instrument that reads the direction and speed of wind and rain clouds to plot a storm's path.

h: Shah's offer: ready to call a special session on SIR
dek: In Hyderabad the home minister dared Rahul Gandhi to a debate, and the Congress stayed away from it.
body: Home Minister Amit Shah led the BJP's 'Save Democracy, Remove Anarchy' march in Hyderabad on Monday and hit back at the opposition's 'vote theft' charge. He said the government is ready to call a special session of Parliament on the voter list issue, and dared Rahul Gandhi to a debate in the House.

Shah said that if the session is called, Prime Minister Narendra Modi will 'break the Congress into pieces'. He called Sunday's Ramlila Maidan rally a 'save the infiltrators' rally. He also asked how the Congress won in Telangana, Kerala, Tamil Nadu and Himachal Pradesh if the EVMs are faulty.

He called Rahul Gandhi's claim of 13 crore names cut wrong. According to Shah, 6.15 crore people have moved elsewhere, about three crore have died, one crore names are duplicates, and three crore are those who do not exist at all. He called them Bangladeshi infiltrators. Shah then said the BJP would remove every infiltrator from the voter list. According to the report, the Congress did not agree to the debate.

Shah kept up his counter-attack on the Congress. He said the Congress does not let Parliament run, and made fun of Rahul Gandhi's foreign trips. He said there were scams worth Rs 12 lakh crore in the Congress's ten years, while there is not a single charge of corruption in Modi's twelve.
nazar: Daring someone to a debate is easy, fixing a date is hard. If a session is called, the government will also have to say on what basis three crore names were removed from the voter list and what the route for checking them is. The point of a debate should not be to corner a leader but to answer the ordinary person whose name was cut by mistake.
sawal: Which count produced the figure of three crore infiltrators?
ref: Special session
A session of Parliament called outside the scheduled calendar on a single issue; the central government sets the date.
SIR
Special Intensive Revision of the voter list, in which names and documents are checked house to house and suspect names are removed.

h: Imran Khan asks the High Court for an unconditional apology
dek: The court said the right to protest belongs only to citizens, and the actor has given in writing that he will not join any demonstration in future.
body: The Bombay High Court on Monday scolded actor Imran Khan for joining a protest in Mumbai over the chief election commissioner and the voters' list. The court said the fundamental right to protest belongs only to Indian citizens. After that the actor apologised without conditions.

The bench of Chief Justice Mahesh Chandra Tripathi and Justice Advait Sethna said OCI cardholders cannot demand the same rights as Indian citizens and that they are 'at the mercy of the country'. The bench also said that instead of ordering Imran to leave the country at once, giving him a notice was India's generosity.

The actor's lawyer Venkatesh Dhond apologised at once and gave in writing that he would not join any protest in future. The court adjourned the hearing on his petition to 7 December and also extended the stay on the FRRO notice.

The row began on 10 October, when Mumbai police took Imran into custody for a while at a protest near August Kranti Maidan. On a complaint by BJP leader Kirit Somaiya, the FRRO issued a notice on 14 October asking him to leave the country by 28 October. Imran had told the court that he had neither called the protest nor taken part in it, that he was present nearby and left when the police asked him to.
nazar: How much right a foreign citizen has to take part in political protest in India is for the court to decide. But this case has made one thing clear: citizenship and civil rights run on separate tracks, and standing up against the election commission can now become a reason to check anyone's foreign papers.
sawal: If an OCI card rests on the country's mercy, who has the right to protest?
ref: OCI card
A document given to people of Indian origin who hold foreign citizenship; it lets them live and work in the country, but gives no right to vote.
FRRO
Foreigners Regional Registration Office, which handles residence, notices and exit for foreign nationals.

h: In Dhubri, bulldozers bring down the homes of 550 families
dek: More than 50 bulldozers were used in the operation in Alamganj, which began at six in the morning on 650 bighas of land.
body: In Assam's Dhubri district, an anti-encroachment drive in the ninth block of Alamganj on Sunday left around 550 families homeless. The administration deployed more than 50 bulldozers on 650 bighas of land, where four thousand people lived. The operation began at six in the morning along with a heavy police force. People were seen weeping and kept praying at the mosque and the shrine.

Dhubri district commissioner Dibakar Nath said there are about 800 families on a total of 800 bighas, and the cases of 160 petitioners on 150 bighas are pending in court. He said the administration will file an affidavit in court and will proceed as per the Gauhati High Court's directions. He called the operation peaceful.

According to the administration, about 80 per cent of the people had packed up and left before the drive. Those who did not show documents were told to vacate the land in 15 days. Electricity to the houses had been cut a few days earlier, so that people would leave. Some families went to court, and their hearing is on 13 November. The school and the shrine were not demolished.

The drive is part of a chain of such operations in Assam. About two weeks earlier, more than 1,100 Muslim families were removed from forest land in Nagaon, Hojai and Golaghat in two days. Human rights organisations have warned that cornering Bengali Muslims in this way can go as far as discrimination.
nazar: The matter is pending in court, and yet the bulldozers moved. The administration should say clearly whether the homes of the 160 families whose papers are in court are standing today. Turning a lack of papers into a crime and leaving thousands on the road is not justice, it is the administration's haste.
sawal: If the case is in court, why did the bulldozers move?
ref: Bigha
An old unit for measuring land; in Assam one bigha is taken as about 0.13 hectare.
Affidavit
A written statement given to a court by a party to a case, signed by that party, which becomes part of the case.

h: Centre tells court Nicobari leaders need not be made parties
dek: The Ministry of Tribal Affairs told the Calcutta High Court that their inclusion in the forest rights petition is not needed.
body: Nicobari leaders trying to join a petition that challenges the settlement of forest rights on Great Nicobar island have been called 'neither necessary nor proper parties' by the Union Ministry of Tribal Affairs. According to court papers, the ministry said these leaders 'slept over their rights through the entire legal process' and their argument should be 'dismissed outright'.

The petition of former IAS officer Meena Gupta is being heard in the Calcutta High Court. It challenges the government's claim that forest rights on the island were settled under the Forest Rights Act 2005. On 9 July 2026, four Nicobari residents applied to join the petition. They say the government certificate refers to village councils of non-tribal settlers, in which no Nicobari was present.

Nicobari and Shompen tribal people live on the island. According to official documents, on 26 July 2022 the lieutenant governor set up a sub-divisional level committee, on 12 August a 'special' village council passed a proposal to swap 166 square kilometres of forest land, and the next day the committee said no one's rights were being taken away.

On 16 August, a no-objection certificate signed by tribal council chief Barnabas Manju was attached to the committee's minutes. In November 2022, Manju withdrew his consent and wrote to the environment ministry that the certificate had been read to him only in part, and that he had not been told what the swap of forest land would mean for the plan to return his ancestors' village.
nazar: A law meant to protect tribal land is being used to argue that tribal people should be kept out of the case, and that is startling. A port, a city and an airport are being built on Great Nicobar, and the people whose land all this is happening on cannot speak in court. That is a weakness of democracy.
sawal: Why were they stopped from fighting for their own land?
ref: Forest Rights Act
A 2005 law that recognises the old rights of adivasis and other communities living in forests.
Shompen
Great Nicobar's tribal community that has very little contact with outsiders, and which the government treats as particularly vulnerable.

h: Parents seek handwriting test on Sahil's apology letter
dek: The parents say their son did not write the apology, and a page is missing from the exam answer sheet as well.
body: After the death of IIT Bombay student Sahil Wakode on 18 September, his parents have asked for a forensic examination of the handwriting of the apology letter that Sahil is said to have written after being caught cheating in an exam. The parents were recently allowed under the Atrocities Act to see the documents seized by the crime branch, and they raised this demand after that.

Father Ravindra Wakode said his son did not write the apology. The institute has maintained that Sahil was caught copying in the exam and then gave a written apology. A delegation of parents and Congress leaders led by Varsha Gaikwad met the state director general of police on Monday and submitted a written demand on their behalf.

The family alleges that a page is missing from the answer sheet of the 18 September exam. According to lawyer Siddharth Ingale, the printed answer sheet had only five questions and the page with the third question is not in the documents, which was brought to the notice of the investigating officer. The letter to the director general of police asks for details of the date of seizure, the person responsible, the number of pages, the seal and further handling.

The parents have also asked for the interim report of the institute's internal committee. In a letter to the Board of Governors sent through their lawyer on Saturday, they said they are not an 'unrelated third party' and have a right to see the report. They have also sought a probe into the missing CCTV footage from the campus.
nazar: A family that has lost its son is having to prove whether the apology was written by him or not. If a page of the answer sheet is missing and CCTV footage cannot be found either, how will trust in the investigation be built? Turning a student's death first into a cheating case and then showing such carelessness with evidence, the two together make the question heavier.
sawal: Where did the page with the third question go?
ref: Atrocities Act
The SC-ST (Prevention of Atrocities) Act, under which the victim's side has the right to copies of the investigation and to documents.
Board of Governors
The top management body of institutions such as the IITs, which keeps an eye on the director and the institution's policies.

h: A blacksmith's shop: tools, and deer as well
dek: In Goalpara in Birbhum, a 49-year-old blacksmith makes tools to run his family; there is no time for art, and coal has become three times dearer.
body: In West Bengal's Birbhum district, Uday Karmakar's workshop is a mud hut under a shirish tree by the road that goes to the Kopai river. His name, painted by hand on the wall, tells you a blacksmith works here. Uday, 49, makes banoti, khunti, kodali and kaste from morning to evening, tools that serve both farming and the kitchen.

But tools are not the whole of the art in his hands. From iron sheet he cuts leaves that can be turned into decorative trays. Deer, elephants and bowls lie on a wooden table by the road for sale. Small pieces go for 100 to 150 rupees and larger, finer pieces for up to 500 rupees.

Smithing is the old trade of his community, and Uday learnt it from his father. His father died of tuberculosis when he was about 12, so going to school did not happen. Most blacksmiths in the area have now taken to repairing bicycles, because Santiniketan and the Visva-Bharati campus are close by and the bicycle is the common ride here.

The work no longer brings a profit. Coal has gone from 12 to 13 rupees a kilo to 30 to 50 rupees a kilo, and scrap comes at 50 to 60 rupees a kilo. Uday works from eight in the morning to eight at night, with a two-hour break at noon. His wife Zaba cleans the pieces, polishes them and applies colour, and his daughter Pooja suggests new designs.

Uday says his heart is in making deer and idols, but that alone will not run a house. He has a state government certificate from an art competition, but the market is not paying the price of his skill.
nazar: A village craftsman cannot stay alive on his art, and this story is not a lone one. Coal, scrap and hard work all get dearer, while the price of something made by hand stays the same.
Tourism has reached here, but its benefit has not reached the craftsman. If skill is kept limited to cheap tools, the next generation will only repair bicycles.
sawal: If these hands can make a deer, why should they make only hoes?
ref: Kamarshal
A blacksmith's workplace, where the forge, the hammer and the material are kept.
Banoti and kodali
Banoti is an iron tool for cutting and chopping, and kodali is a hoe-like tool used for digging.

h: A Muslim trans woman, priest of a Hindu goddess's temple
dek: At Thiruvalam in Vellore, Bhai Amma has run the Angala Amman temple for three decades, where people come without anyone asking caste or religion.
body: At the end of a mud road in Thiruvalam, in Tamil Nadu's Vellore district, stands a temple that people call Bhai Amma's temple. Bhai Amma, 57, is a Muslim trans woman and the chief priest of the goddess Angala Amman. Devotees queued up on Tuesday too, and Bhai Amma answers every question by throwing 18 cowrie shells.

Each session costs 600 rupees and comes with a bag of coconut, banana, vermilion and lemon. Bhai Amma listens to people's troubles and gives plain advice. She tells one man not to call back the woman who left him, and tells another to take his daughter to a doctor rather than marry her off early.

Her real name is Rahman Basha, and in the trans community she is Razia Begum. She comes from the Labbai Muslim community, goes to the mosque with her family on Ramzan and Bakrid, and wants to be buried with Islamic rites when she dies. At the same time she worships the goddess, because in her view neither comes in the way of the other.

At 12 she was cooking in a hotel and in the evening would light a lamp and tell the goddess about people's troubles. At 22, with the landowner's permission, she began building the temple here, and the main sanctum was built in the 2000s. At first there was opposition from both the Hindu and the Muslim side, and some people accused her of cheating.

Today people of every caste, religion and gender come here, and the crowd swells at the Maina Kollai festival. Bhai Amma wants another trans woman to take over the temple's work. But her papers still describe her as a man and a Muslim.
nazar: That a temple's money, rituals and employment are all in the hands of a trans woman is hard even to imagine in the villages of north India. Here the one society kept furthest outside broke the boundary of religion itself.
But there is another question. When her papers do not recognise her identity, then after the temple, in what name will she fight for land, a bank account and the law?
sawal: Why is the goddess's priest not in her own papers?
ref: Thirunangai
The word used in Tamil Nadu for trans women, who have fought a long struggle for identity and rights.
Maina Kollai
A folk festival held in Tamil Nadu, in which devotees ask the goddess for favours by punishing the body.

h: Bodies cut by cane: 10 lakh workers, only 304 accidents on record
dek: Sugarcane workers in Maharashtra work 14 to 16 hours a day for six months; bodies break, but only 304 accidents ever reached the compensation office.
body: Sitting in her hut in Ahrawahegaon in Beed district, Sita Sasane says that in October 2023, while cutting cane in a field in Kolhapur, her husband Keshav's face twisted to one side and he fell down.

The doctor said he had a stroke. But the family could not go to hospital, because they had taken an advance of one and a half lakh rupees from the contractor, which was to be cut from the cane they harvested over six months. The contractor did not let them go for three days. In the end it was settled that Suraj would stay in the field and the others would take Keshav away.

Maharashtra makes about 35 per cent of the country's sugar. From November, about 10 lakh workers work in these fields for six months, the day runs 14 to 16 hours and they live in tents in the field itself. In a 2016 study, half the workers in Ahilyanagar reported back pain, and in a 2013 study, two out of three had been injured by a sickle or a cane stump.

In October 2024 the state government started a scheme for compensation in case of disability or death in an accident. Government figures from 2024 to 2026 mention the deaths of 186 workers, 112 seriously injured and six left disabled, and more than 10 crore rupees paid out as compensation. That is 304 serious accidents in two years. Activists call this very low, because putting together the papers for compensation is impossible.

Shankar Waghmare of Kathoda village in Beed fell off a tractor four years ago and still walks with a limp from a spinal injury, and he does not even know that the government has started a compensation scheme. Activist Manisha Tokle says most workers are not registered at all and the contractor gives no certificate.
nazar: The profit of the sugar industry is shared between mills and contractors, and the whole risk sits on the worker's body. The advance of one and a half lakh that ties a family down is recorded nowhere on paper, and all the proof for compensation stays in the contractor's hands.
Making a scheme is not enough. Registration of workers must be compulsory, the responsibility of both mill and contractor must be fixed, and quick treatment must open to everyone.
sawal: The body that makes sugar, which account holds its cost?
ref: Advance
Money paid by the contractor before the season, which is cut from the value of the cane harvested; workers stay tied to it until they leave.
Musculoskeletal disorder
A disorder of muscles, joints and bones caused by repeating the same movement, which grows slowly.

h: The flood water went down, the women's fear did not
dek: In Kerala's coastal villages the 2018 flood and the tidal flooding that returns every year broke women from within; relief came from community theatre.
body: Puthenvelikkara village in Ernakulam district lies between the Periyar and Chalakudy rivers, ringed by tidal ponds and backwaters. People here are used to water coming every December, but the 2018 flood was different. In 57-year-old Sailaja's house the water rose six to eight feet and the family stayed scattered for three days.

That flood was Kerala's biggest in a hundred years. More than 400 people died, lakhs were displaced and the state suffered losses of more than 10,000 crore rupees. Sailaja's son Abhimanyu spent 48 hours on the roof and celebrated his 24th birthday in a relief camp.

Community theatre became the way to deal with this shock. The play, called Chevitthorama, was put together by ten people from the same village, none of whom had acted before. It was made with Manjula Bharati of the Tata Institute of Social Sciences along with the organisation Equinoct, and directed by Sreejit Ramanan of the School of Drama in Thrissur.

The tidal flood that comes every year is a different kind of tiredness for women. It slowly eats away home, well, work and mind. Vilasini, 63, was living on MGNREGA wages after her husband lost his job when his hand was cut in a coir factory, and her sons' auto did not run for months.

In 2026 the state government has declared tidal flooding a state-specific disaster. The mental health organisation MHAT is currently helping 57 such people and their families. Kerala started a district mental health programme back in 1999, but doctors accept that medicine alone does not settle the matter.
nazar: Disaster figures count houses, crops and cattle, not the mind. When women hold a family together, their own fear gets pushed somewhere, and that same fear returns years later as illness.

In such a situation, things like theatre are not a show, they are treatment. If government help stays limited to compensation, women in coastal villages will keep bearing the same shock with every tide.
sawal: The flood returns every year, so who treats the fear?
ref: Tidal flooding
Sea water entering settlements through rivers and drains with the tide, which happens every year in Kerala's coastal areas.
Chevitthorama
A local Catholic ritual of blowing a prayer into the ear of a dying person, after which the play is named.

h: Workers going back to Poland: they earned in Germany, not a life
dek: This DW film follows the Polish workers who spent years in Germany and are now returning, because rent, prices and bureaucracy have upset the arithmetic they had relied on to stay there.
body: Tomasz has been driving trucks in Berlin for more than ten years. The work is fine, but rent and the cost of food and water have risen so fast that the monthly account has begun to go wrong. In the film he says that as soon as his daughter finishes school, he will go back to Poland with his family. This is not a decision taken suddenly, it is the result of years of counting.

The film's story begins with a student. Filip Panek enrolled at Viadrina University in Frankfurt (Oder) on the German-Polish border, hoping to build a career in Germany after his studies. Now his plan has changed and he is getting ready to finish his legal traineeship in Poland. There he sees not only family and friends but new economic opportunities too.

On the other side stands Michael Sünkler, who runs a transport company and has many Polish employees. In the last few years several of them have gone back. For him this is not a political debate, it is an everyday economic crisis: people to drive trucks, run machines and look after others are getting hard to find.

Kamila Gierko and her husband Zbigniew Perzyna have already taken the decision. Six months ago they returned from Berlin to Szczecin in Poland. For years they had good conditions for doing their own work in Germany, but slowly paperwork, the lack of digital services, high taxes and the burden of social security began to weigh on them. After returning they feel both their time and their money are being saved.

The film also asks why Germany is losing the pull that drew Polish workers until a decade ago. Poland's economy has grown fast, wages there are rising and new openings for work are being created in cities. When decent earnings and a sense of belonging are available at home, the account of the nights spent abroad begins to be recast.

There is another side to this too: going back is not always easy. For those who have built a home, their children's school and a circle of friends in Germany, return is a new beginning, in which job, house and identity all have to be built again. Through these people's voices the film raises the same question every worker carries with him: where is the earning more, and where is life.

For India this story is familiar. Our workers in the Gulf and in Europe also return after years, sometimes to build a house with their savings, sometimes in illness or old age. Until there is a job with respect, a fixed wage and social security here at home, returning will remain a compulsion, not a choice.
nazar: People who go from one country to another to work first weigh the cost of living and the bureaucracy. When that arithmetic goes wrong, the decision to return is economic, not one of patriotism. The film puts this plain fact in front of us.

The direct lesson for India is that migrant workers should not be seen only as a channel for sending foreign exchange. They should have a place to return to, recognition of their skills and security in old age; only then will their return become a decision of their own will.
sawal: Why do people head home the moment the wage gap narrows?
ref: Viadrina University
A university in Frankfurt (Oder) on the border between Germany and Poland, known for students from both countries.
Szczecin
A port city in north-west Poland, about a hundred and fifty kilometres from Berlin, where returning workers begin a new life.

h: The room's things start talking: a teenager's night, audited
dek: In sixteen-year-old Aarush Mishra's story, at three in the morning the school bag, chair, table and bookshelf sit down to settle accounts with their owner's lazy life.
body: The story 'Kamra Raat Mein' (The Room at Night), published in Sammukh, is by sixteen-year-old Aarush Mishra. It is three in the morning, the moon is up, and its light slips through the gap between the curtains and falls on the table, the chair and the bag. The teenager on the bed is snoring, but his room is not asleep.

The first to speak is the school bag, called 'basta-ustad' in the story. He tries to light a piece of chalk like a beedi and keeps throwing the other things' complaints into the fire he has made. The chair grieves over a week of sweaty clothes, the table over the fact that the boy's mother does all the housework while this monster does nothing, and the bookshelf over a promise broken every month to keep the books in order.

The room's things speak in village dialect, and that is the funniest part of the story. The computer, the AC, the pillow, the diary and an unfinished page pressed under the table also have their say. All agree on one thing: this boy does not go out to play, he mutters to himself late into the night and stays tangled in stories of his own making.

In the middle of this council that runs all night, the teenager survives on his diary, which holds restless words written for someone. The whole story takes place in one room, yet in that room the full temper of a teenager, his laziness, his mischief and his tangled feeling all come into view.

Sammukh has published the story with a comment by the poet and teacher Sudipti. She writes that the boy reads a great deal in both Hindi and English, but his creativity flowers more in Hindi, and that she is among the first readers of this story.
nazar: The big thing is not that a sixteen-year-old boy writes a story, but that he gave his own room a place to speak. Young writers are visible in numbers in Hindi, but the places that publish them are few. When schoolboys and schoolgirls get a stage, the language survives and finds its own tongue outside the imitation of English.
sawal: If the things in your room started talking, what would they say first?
ref: Basta-ustad
The name given to the school bag in the story, which tries to set a piece of chalk smouldering like a beedi.
Sardar Patel Vidyalaya
An old school in Delhi, where the story's writer studies in class eleven.

h: A warrant for being a rebel: poems published for the first time
dek: Sammukh has published Vallari Srivastava's poems for the first time, in which the grief of losing someone close, a charge of sedition and the symbols of nature move together.
body: Sammukh has published several poems by Vallari Srivastava, and the magazine itself writes that this is her first publication. What catches the eye at the very first reading is the stillness. The words do not move in a hurry, they move at the pace of living a memory again.

The first poem circles the death of someone close. A piece of sweet, a tin of jaggery, a paan gillauri, white batasha, a muslin kurta and a hill stream, all return in the same memory. The poem speaks of stroking skin that has already gone cold one last time. The sorrow of this poem does not shout, it sees someone off quietly.

'Tumhare Baagi Hone Ka' (About your being a rebel) suddenly carries you to another world. Someone has received a sedition notice, and instead of arguing about it the poet stands on his side. In 'Ishwar Ka Chehra' (God's face) faith and fear move together, where angels are seen turning into vultures and a woman is given only trust, not a soul.

The sea, a river, a clump of bamboo, the lines on the skin of a thumb and a spring growing inside, a large part of these poems comes from nature. But nature here is not decoration, it is a way of telling the state of the mind. In one poem an unarmed sea sits in a corner, with nothing left but the stubbornness to return.
Sammukh has written about these poems that they show not playfulness but the continuity of a writer's practice, and the magazine has wished for her poetic future.
nazar: Reading a new poet, the best thing seems to be that she does not try to make her sorrow big. Home, the death of someone close, a paan gillauri and the sea, all are so easy that the reader feels he is going back to his own memories. Such voices are not new in Hindi poetry, but every new voice brings a new home with it.
sawal: Where does so much stillness come from in a poem published for the first time?
ref: Paan gillauri
A sweet ball wrapped in a betel leaf and put in the mouth, which children love to eat.
Sedition
A charge brought for writing or speaking against the government, in which bail is hard.
photo_note: Muhammad Ali, 'A Beauty in a Garden', Mughal miniature

h: Waiting for Aabai: the one who taught me to write 'ka'
dek: An adivasi grandmother in Nepal's Surkhet, who put five daughters through school and went to court for land, is now counting her breaths in an ICU.
body: In Hindwi's 'Bela', Pawan Thapa writes about his aabai, his maternal grandmother. She was from Biju village in Nepal's Surkhet, the youngest wife of the head of the household and the middle daughter-in-law. When her youngest daughter was born, she was kept apart from the house, not even given a plate to eat from, only for having given birth to daughters.

Aabai built a hut in Baddichaur with four daughters and gave birth to the youngest there. She was illiterate herself, but she set her mind on educating her daughters. When her husband did not support her, she sold a little grain and liquor to arrange clothes, books and fees. The writer notes that the thinking of that time, that daughters should be married off rather than educated, was challenged by Aabai alone.

Her father-in-law gave her land but not its purja, the ownership document. When the daughters did not get their share, Aabai went to court and came back with the right. The writer believes it was her rebellious consciousness that came into him too. The woman who had never held a copy or a pen took his hand and taught him to write 'ka', and taught him to love grain, trees and soil.

This boy, raised without a father, had to hear even 'a child with no father' in the village. Once he asked Aabai what it would have been like to have a father. Aabai took him in her lap and wept late into the night, and the writer never repeated that question.

In the end there is the ICU. The operation is over and the chance of survival is put at five per cent. The doctors say blood has clotted in the brain and artificial breathing will only increase the suffering, and the family has to decide. The writer can only say that she should be laid not in a hospital but at home, under the kimu tree that Aabai raised along with him.
nazar: This memoir matters because it is the story of a woman who sat in no council and was counted in no movement, yet by educating her daughters and her grandson she did work that big speeches cannot do. At the same time, let it be remembered that keeping an old person in an ICU or not is often decided by a poor family's money, not by love.
sawal: The one who taught me 'ka', why should we decide her last breath?
ref: Surkhet
A district in mid-western Nepal, where farmers and adivasi communities live in large numbers around the Karnali river.
Bulaki
An ornament worn in the nose, which Aabai wore and which the writer danced to see.

h: Binoy Majumdar: poetry that grew between the formulas of mathematics
dek: Baby Shaw examines the Bengali poet Binoy Majumdar's diaries, 'Gayatri Ke', and the obsession out of which the Hungry Generation was born.
body: Baby Shaw's article in Bela circles the Bengali poet Binoy Majumdar (1934-2006), but it begins with a letter. In August 1962 Shakti Chattopadhyay wrote to Binoy that while reading the poems of his collection 'Gayatri Ke' the thought of 'hunger' came to mind, and from that thought the 'Kshudharta Andolan', the Hungry Generation, was founded.

'Gayatri Ke' had sixteen poems. Later Binoy spread the same love over seventy-seven poems and wrote 'Phire Eso, Chaka', which is regarded in Bengali poetry as a remarkable book of love. The writer asks who this Gayatri was. From several people she learnt that she was Gayatri Chakravorty, a brilliant student of Presidency College in the fifties, who came to be known later as Gayatri Chakravorty Spivak.

Binoy had not even been properly introduced to her. Even so he kept writing from Durgapur asking for her address, and kept requesting everyone from Shakti to Salil Chakraborty. Salil replied plainly that it was better to drop this curiosity about why he needed Gayatri.

The article cites his diaries, where mathematics formulas are at the bottom and lines of poetry at the top, and somewhere 'Bhalobasa abashisht nei' is written, meaning 'no love is left'. He had a deep mathematical mind, studied engineering, worked at the Indian Statistical Institute and taught at Tripura Government College, but on the way to poetry he gave up that path.

The writer says mathematics gave him the habit of looking at things and searching for their structure, and poetry opened the world where feeling, reason and the limits of formula begin to dissolve. She has also done the Hindi translation of the poetry lines and letters in this column herself.
nazar: This article matters because instead of repeating the image of the poet's 'madness', it looks at the room where obsession turns into loneliness. It also leaves the question of why the women in whose names poems are written never get a place in that love themselves. Gayatri Chakravorty Spivak, whom Binoy barely knew, remained the 'goddess' of his seventy-seven poems.
sawal: The women in whose names poems were written, when were they asked what they wanted?
ref: Hungry Generation
A Bengali literary movement of the sixties, also called the Kshudharta Andolan, which made hunger a large metaphor.
Gayatri Chakravorty Spivak
A philosopher and translator of Indian origin, who translated Jacques Derrida's 'Of Grammatology' into English.

h: Sir Syed's yardstick: technology fast, where is the ethics
dek: In an essay that won a prize at Aligarh's essay competition, Musharraf Parwez asks 21st-century questions of technology from a 19th-century reformer.
body: Musharraf Parwez wrote this essay for the Sir Syed Day essay competition at Aligarh Muslim University, in which he won this year's prize in Hindi. The university holds the competition every year, the essays carry no author's name, and the selected essays were given awards on 17 October.

The essay's question is what Sir Syed's dream of a rational society means in the 21st century. The writer recalls that Sir Syed opposed evils such as purdah, polygamy and sati, wrote a book on the causes of the 1857 revolt, founded the Scientific Society in 1864, brought out Tahzib-ul-Akhlaq, and in 1877 opened the college that later became Aligarh Muslim University.

Then come the numbers. According to the information agency PIB's figures for June 2025, India had 93.3 crore telephone connections in March 2014 and by April 2025 the number had crossed 120 crore. The internet came to the country in August 1995 and today about 95.8 crore people are active internet users, of whom nearly 57 per cent are in villages.

But the writer says the relation between power and trust also runs the other way. According to the cyber crime coordination centre's figures for January 2026, Indians lost about 52,976 crore rupees in the last six years to cases such as online fraud, investment scams and digital arrests. That is why he returns to Sir Syed's argument that no piece of information should be accepted without checking.
In the end his argument is that technology is not the goal but the means, and the task of education is not only to prepare people for employment but to give them judgement as well.
nazar: The weakness of this essay is that it was written for a prize platform, so there is more praise of Sir Syed and fewer questions. But the figure on which it stops is itself a question. When half the country's villages have come onto the internet, literacy should mean not just reading but recognising a lie. Sir Syed's real test is being held today in a government school classroom, not at a ceremony.
sawal: Is 52 thousand crore of fraud the price of technology?
ref: Tahzib-ul-Akhlaq
Sir Syed's Urdu newspaper, started in 1870, which carried writing on social reform and reason.
Muhammadan Anglo-Oriental College
The college opened in Aligarh in 1877, which later became Aligarh Muslim University.

h: Chandni Chowk's shared culture: now in a guide's telling
dek: Reading Rajinder Arora's book 'Purani Dilli: Sajha Sanskriti Ka Safar', Hariyash Rai recalls a world of bazaars, places of worship and flavours.
body: In this review published in Shabdankan, Hariyash Rai reads Rajinder Arora's book 'Purani Dilli: Sajha Sanskriti Ka Safar' (Old Delhi: A Journey of Shared Culture), which Vam Prakashan has brought out. Arora is known as a graphic designer and mountaineer, and the foreword to the book is by film director Rakesh Omprakash Mehra.

The book looks at Delhi not as a list of monuments but as everyday shared life. Arora notes that Shahjahan's mother, Jagat Gosain, was from a Hindu royal family and her original name was Manibai. In his court, thirty-five Hindu mansabdars held positions from five hundred to five thousand. The book also records that Holi and Diwali were celebrated inside the Red Fort.

The second home of the shared culture is Chandni Chowk, which Aurangzeb's sister Jahanara founded. Arora writes that it was not only goods that were bought and sold there, culture was served too. Then times changed, the British came, havelis were pulled down in the name of widening roads, and the bazaar's quiet elegance filled with crowds, noise and smoke.

What the reviewer remembers most are the shops of Karim and Javed Nihari, where he meets Brahmins who eat vegetables all year and fall upon mutton on Eid. That is the book's strength: before big claims, it talks of brotherhood through flavours and shops.

Arora also accepts that the same thread kept running in the new Hindustan. Customers moved to malls and online shopping, and shopkeepers shy away from coming there even three generations later. What is left is old walls, dust and a half-finished memory.
nazar: The importance of such books is that they take history out of a list of years and battles and bring it down to a lane, a shop and a sweet. But while writing about a shared culture, it should also be remembered that it never rested on equality. In the same bazaar everyone had shops, but the places people lived and the neighbourhoods stayed separate. That point is thin in this review, which makes the sharedness too quickly calm and beautiful.
sawal: Chandni Chowk's shared culture, whose responsibility is it today?
ref: Vam Prakashan
A Delhi publishing house that brings out books on history, culture and travel.
Jahanara Begum
Shahjahan's daughter, who had the Chandni Chowk market built in Shahjahanabad.
